title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded in per‑task artifacts and thus could not be evaluated. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We present preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, complete numeric outcomes, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and implications.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being actively explored for NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1,2]. Stochastic generation can produce syntactic or semantic violations—missing commands, unsafe operation orderings, or constraint breaches—that create operational risk when applied to device CLIs. To mitigate such risk, research and prototype pipelines propose interposing deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analyses) and bounded repair loops—generate–verify–repair (GVR)—so that only outputs passing a deterministic oracle are considered safe to apply [3–5]. Prior work has described components and small prototypes, but preregistered, paired evaluations that instrument verifier‑triggered repair benefit with archived deterministic traces are limited [1–3].

Motivated by this gap, we asked: Does a GVR pipeline that uses a single sampled initial LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), a deterministic Batfish‑style validator, and at most one automated LLM repair call reduce verifier‑detected semantic/safety failures relative to the same initial candidate without repair? Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation executed under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints. We preserve the exact preregistered estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), report exact execution accounting, provide representative before/after artifacts, and discuss statistical interpretation and validity threats specific to shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.related_work: LLM applications in NetOps include intent→CLI translation systems and benchmark efforts that study automated configuration generation and correctness [1]. Surveys and tutorials summarize opportunities and failure modes for LLMs in network operations and AIOps, arguing for grounding and verification components when moving toward automation [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed in code generation and regulated domains to produce deterministic validation guarantees via external oracles and repair loops [3]. Network verification tools such as Batfish and header‑space analyses are frequently suggested as verifier components inside LLM‑driven pipelines because they can perform reachability and required‑sequence checks that are deterministic given a network model [4]. Prior research on LLM needs for correct router configuration highlights the difficulty of ensuring correct sequencing and vendor‑specific syntax, motivating verifier augmentation [5]. Our work differs by executing a preregistered paired test that (a) uses shared_initial_candidate semantics per the preregistration, (b) archives raw model traces and deterministic validator traces for auditability, and (c) reports paired contingency counts and exact tests consistent with the registered analysis plan.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration is cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under those semantics the same single sampled initial model candidate is used to compute both the baseline outcome (single‑shot candidate → deterministic validator pass/fail) and the guarded outcome (same candidate → verifier; if it fails, at most one automated LLM repair is permitted; final verifier pass/fail recorded).

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered task bank deterministically produced 300 intent→CLI pairs (150 Cisco‑like; 150 Juniper‑like) using a published deterministic synthetic task generator and public NetConfEval‑style examples; generation seeds, task generator id, and per‑task manifest entries are archived. Inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration. Deterministic exclusions removed 34 both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures, leaving 266 complete paired units for the primary analysis (complete_pairs = 266).

Model and orchestration: The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Archived configuration fields (model_configuration.json) include max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). The archived null temperature is not evidence that sampling was deterministic (temperature=0); no deterministic sampling seed was archived, so recorded outputs may include nondeterministic sampling. The orchestration adapter used was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 (archived adapter family). Provider_call_audit in the reconciliation artifact records hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34. Stage accounting records shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6 (six repair calls occurred across the full planned set).

Deterministic validator: The experiment used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the binary oracle. The validator performs: syntactic parsing of CLI lines, normalization of command forms, required‑sequence checks against task payload expected sequences, constrained field touch checks (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields), and reachability/constraint checks on the synthetic topology model. Its outcome is a binary pass/fail for the primary endpoint; detailed validator traces (validation_before, validation_after) are archived per episode, including observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation codes, and normalized_configuration.

Execution contract and repair loop: Per the preregistration, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate. For each task exactly one initial generation call was produced (shared across baseline and guarded). If the validator failed that candidate the guarded arm could invoke at most one automated LLM repair call (the repair prompt and repair_provider_trace are archived where used). Repair design was a bounded one‑step automated LLM prompt that exposed the validator’s failure codes and asked for a corrected configuration that satisfies the task manifest constraints; repair calls occurred only when the deterministic validator return indicated failure.

Analysis plan: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes (preregistered α=0.05). For interval estimation we preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference; we report both because the exact McNemar test uses only discordant counts (a discrete finite‑sample statistic) while bootstrap CIs incorporate resampling variability and can provide complementary information about magnitude and uncertainty. Secondary estimands included median_repair_iterations_per_task and (preregistered) median end‑to‑end latency per task (the latter could not be evaluated because per‑episode latency was not recorded). Missingness: 34 both‑arm provider failures were excluded from the primary confirmatory analysis per the preregistered missingness_plan; sensitivity analyses treated missing pairs conservatively as failures in both arms and are reported below.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 task pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68; complete paired units analysed = 266 (both_missing_pairs = 34). Model calls used = 306 (provider_call_audit). Repair stage calls recorded = 6 (repair stage_count = 6). Completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (complete_pairs = 266): baseline successes = 260; guarded (final GVR) successes = 265. Observed contingency counts: n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed proportions: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Paired difference = 0.01879699248. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered decision rule α=0.05 → not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. The bootstrap CI was computed according to the registered bootstrap parameters and archived (analysis_log.jsonl). The apparent discrepancy—an exact McNemar p > 0.05 alongside a bootstrap CI that excludes zero—stems from discrete finite‑sample behavior: exact McNemar is a test based solely on discordant counts (here n10=5, n01=0) and has discrete possible p‑values; resampling CIs summarize empirical paired‑difference variability and can exclude zero in small‑discordant settings even when an exact two‑sided test fails to meet α.

Repair behavior and representative artifacts: Repair was invoked 6 times across the 300 planned tasks (repair stage_count = 6). Median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2(a) confirmed). Representative artifact example: task-000008 shared initial response (baseline) contained a truncated final line "interface uplink2\n" (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt, sha256 = 89306095ce...), producing an invalid or incomplete configuration; the guarded final artifact (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt, sha256 = d52b7616f...) contains the completed corrected sequence including "interface uplink2 admin down" and the subsequent edge1 commands, illustrating a repair that completed a missing command and restored the required sequence. All episode validator traces for task-000008 are archived in the scoring artifacts and show validation_before failing on parsed_command_count mismatch and validation_after passing after repair. Contamination checks: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty; no exact public‑duplicate tasks were flagged and none were excluded for contamination from the primary analysis.

Missingness sensitivity: Treating the 34 both‑arm excluded episodes as failures for a conservative N=300 analysis yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667, guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333, paired difference = 0.016667; discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) remain the same and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. This sensitivity confirms the primary inferential conclusion is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness handling.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The guarded GVR pipeline produced a small absolute increase in verifier pass‑rate on analysed pairs (~1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The practical headroom for improvement was limited because baseline single‑shot pass rate was already very high (≈97.7%), leaving few failing cases for repair to correct. Repair invocations were rare (6/300), indicating that, for this task corpus and model, most single‑shot samples satisfied the deterministic validator.

Implications for pipeline design: When baseline pass rates are high the marginal operational benefit of automated bounded repairs is limited; architectures may instead focus effort on (a) improving first‑pass generation for lower‑baseline‑accuracy task pools, (b) expanding validator coverage to detect more subtle semantic errors, or (c) designing escalation policies that route ambiguous failures to human operators. Our results do not imply that GVR is unnecessary; rather, they quantify a small verifier‑triggered benefit for a high baseline pass corpus under the tested model and validator set.

Threats to validity (brief): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean the estimand measures the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample, not the effect of constrained prompting or multiple independent generations. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a specific rule battery (syntax, required sequences, reachability over synthetic topology) and cannot detect violations outside its coverage; undetected semantic errors are possible. External validity: tasks derive from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor dialect clusters; results may not generalize to larger topologies, other vendors, or production datasets. Conclusion validity: small discordant counts (n10=5, n01=0) produce limited power for exact discrete tests; 34 both‑arm infrastructure failures reduced the analysed sample from 300 to 266 and thereby reduced precision. Runtime nondeterminism: the archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed was archived; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded.

Recommendations: For future confirmatory studies we recommend (i) selecting task corpora with lower baseline pass rates to better measure repair effectiveness; (ii) recording per‑episode end‑to‑end latencies to evaluate operational bounds (the preregistered H2(b) could not be evaluated because per‑episode latency was not archived); (iii) increasing validator coverage (additional reachability or semantic checks) while documenting validator limits; and (iv) evaluating constrained first‑pass prompting or multiple independent draws in a design that deviates from shared_initial_candidate semantics (explicitly preregister such deviations).
sections.conclusion:
A preregistered paired experiment evaluated a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) on intent→CLI tasks under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved verifier pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts, including raw responses, validator traces, provider call accounting, and reconciliation manifests, are archived in the evidence bundle to support reanalysis and follow‑on work.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
